nature-econ-158.title: Economic efficiency: getting the most from what we have
nature-econ-158.text: An economy can be efficient and still deeply unequal. Economic efficiency means getting the most of what people want, such as well-being, out of the resources available. Economists usually mean one of two things by it. The first asks whether any change could help one person without harming another; it is named after Vilfredo Pareto and explored in {{ref:nature-econ-178}}. The second asks whether more of one good could be made without making less of another, at the lowest average cost, the subject of {{ref:nature-econ-200}}. The two need not go together. A market can pass one test and fail the other. Both matter because productive resources are scarce. They must go to each industry in just the right amounts, or too much or too little gets made. Theory says a perfectly competitive equilibrium passes the first test, but only without market imperfections, and these are significant in real markets. Efficiency in this sense says nothing about equality or a society's overall well-being. Removing one distortion does not always help either: if another cannot be removed, efficiency may even fall. Economists also split over who distorts more. One school stresses the distortions governments create; another stresses those markets create and wants more government involvement to fix them. Many economists consider putting a price on carbon, explored in {{ref:nature-pol-239}}, the most efficient way to cut greenhouse gas emissions.

nature-econ-168.title: Pareto efficiency: when no one can gain without someone losing
nature-econ-168.text: Smith owns an apple but wants an orange. Jones owns an orange but wants an apple. A swap makes both better off, so the starting point was wasteful. That small scene captures Pareto efficiency. A situation is Pareto efficient when there is no longer any way to make one person better off without making someone else worse off. A change that helps at least one person and harms nobody is a Pareto improvement, and efficiency is reached once no such change is left. The idea is named after Vilfredo Pareto (1848–1923), an Italian engineer and economist who used it to study economic efficiency and how income is shared. He called it 'optimal', but it does not pick out one best outcome. It marks out a whole set of outcomes, which is why 'efficiency' fits better. Nor does it mean fairness. An economy where a wealthy few hold most resources can still be Pareto efficient. Market failure, in these terms, is a case where markets miss an efficient allocation, so a Pareto improvement is possible. In {{ref:nature-econ-202}} the same idea is called the unanimity principle: if everyone prefers A to B, society should too. In practice, hidden information and the problems it causes make Pareto efficiency hard to judge. So most people do not take the welfare theorems as accurate descriptions of the real world.

nature-econ-159.title: Welfare economics: judging how well off a society is
nature-econ-159.text: How can anyone judge whether a whole society is better or worse off? Welfare economics is the branch of economics that tries, using the tools of microeconomics. It guides the study of how government action can improve social welfare, and it supplies the theory behind {{ref:nature-val-001}}. Two results anchor it. The first fundamental theorem says competitive markets, under certain assumptions, give Pareto efficient outcomes, an idea sometimes linked to Adam Smith's invisible hand. The second says any Pareto efficient outcome can be reached through a competitive market. A planner first makes lump-sum transfers, one-off payments that do not depend on what anyone does. Some count {{ref:nature-econ-179}} as a third. The field has had two eras. Edgeworth, Sidgwick, Marshall and Pigou built the early neoclassical approach. The later approach, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-167}}, rests on the work of Pareto, Kaldor, Hicks and Scitovsky. Pigou's idea of an externality remains central, both here and in environmental economics. Critics push from different sides. Amartya Sen urged welfare research to use a wider range of data and to discuss ethics and morality openly. Austrian school economists reject welfare economics outright, cardinal and ordinal alike, because it relies on comparing different people's utility.

nature-econ-209.title: Utilitarianism: the greatest good for everyone affected
nature-econ-209.text: What is the right thing to do? Utilitarianism gives one answer: whatever produces the most happiness and well-being for everyone affected. Jeremy Bentham founded it. He proposed measuring pleasures and pains by their intensity, duration, certainty and nearness, a method called the hedonic calculus. His successor John Stuart Mill reshaped it and popularized the name, rejecting a purely quantitative measure because some pleasures are worth more than others. In social choice, the utilitarian rule picks the option with the highest sum of everyone's utilities. An offshoot, wealth maximization, allows changes that raise total surplus even if some lose, as long as winners could compensate losers. Its ideas reach welfare economics, justice, global poverty, the ethics of raising animals for food and existential risks, and they underlie Peter Singer's approach to animal ethics. Critics object that well-being cannot be measured or compared. In 1971 Rawls argued that it ignores the distinction between persons.

nature-econ-160.title: Social welfare functions: ranking states of society
nature-econ-160.text: A single shopper can rank two baskets of groceries. Can a whole society rank two ways of sharing out its income? A social welfare function tries to. It is a rule that ranks possible states of society from more to less desirable by combining the preferences of everyone in it. Unlike one consumer's utility function, it maps many people's utility functions onto a single result. Ordinal versions use only whether one option is better than another; cardinal versions also use how much better. Abram Bergson introduced the term in a 1938 article, to state precisely the value judgements needed to define maximum economic welfare. Doubts came early. In 1935 Lionel Robbins argued that changes in different people's utilities cannot be compared by any empirical test. Later, {{ref:nature-econ-179}} showed that a society, unlike a single consumer, cannot build a fully consistent decision rule from ranked preferences alone.

nature-econ-202.title: Social choice theory: turning many wishes into one decision
nature-econ-202.text: Every election is an attempt to turn many wishes into one decision. Social choice theory is the branch of welfare economics that studies how individual preferences can be combined into good collective decisions. It is normative, asking how a society should decide, while political science describes how societies actually decide. Constitutions, parliamentary voting procedures and electoral systems are real social choice rules, so the field is sometimes called voting theory. It began with the Marquis de Condorcet, and Kenneth Arrow's book Social Choice and Individual Values opened its modern era. Two classic rules sit at opposite poles. The utilitarian rule maximizes the sum of utilities; the egalitarian or Rawlsian rule maximizes the smallest. Gibbard's theorem shows that with three or more outcomes, no voting rule can always make honest voting the best strategy. In 1970 Amartya Sen's Collective Choice and Social Welfare brought comparisons between people and the idea of capability into the field. Later work extended it to fair division, legal compensation and natural resources.

nature-econ-196.title: Market distortions: when prices stop telling the truth
nature-econ-196.text: A tax on wages discourages some people from working. That push is a market distortion. The term covers any departure from perfect competition that makes a market settle at a price clearly different from the competitive one. People pursuing their own good then no longer maximize society's welfare. A distortion can be measured as the gap between a good's market price and its marginal social cost. Sources include regulation, monopoly, tariffs and limits on imports, uncorrected externalities, unequal tax rates, inflation and incomplete information. Each can cause a net loss of social surplus. Not every tax distorts. A proportional tax on wages does, because it discourages work; a fixed charge that nothing can change, explored in {{ref:nature-pol-119}}, does not. Distortions are often responses to market failures, the circumstances that prevent perfect competition. They can also be reduced on purpose. Revenue from {{ref:nature-pol-253}} could be used to cut distorting taxes, making climate policy more efficient.

nature-econ-173.title: Distributive justice: who should get what
nature-econ-173.text: Who should get what? Distributive justice is the question of how a society's resources, goods and opportunities should be shared out fairly among its members. Most modern theories start from scarcity: material resources are limited. Their answers differ sharply. Rawls offered one, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-175}}. Others include utilitarianism, the push for equal treatment covered in {{ref:nature-econ-176}}, and the Marxist rule 'from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs'. Applied to the environment, it asks how risks, harms and benefits are shared. Today the burdens fall mostly on the Global South, while benefits go mainly to the Global North. In debates over climate, it asks who bears the costs of climate change and of the actions taken against it. Some reject the idea itself. Friedrich von Hayek called it meaningless in a market system, where outcomes arise spontaneously. Robert Nozick argued in Anarchy, State, and Utopia that the term is not neutral, because no central distributor hands out shares.

nature-econ-178.title: Allocative efficiency: making the goods people want
nature-econ-178.text: Suppose a firm makes 40 units of a good. The 40th costs $6 to make, yet buyers would pay $15 for it. Society would gain from more. Allocative efficiency is the state in which the mix of goods produced matches what people want, so society's welfare is as high as it can be. In that example it is reached at 70 units, where marginal cost equals marginal utility. In general, each good's marginal benefit to consumers must be at least its marginal cost; for a firm in a perfect market, price equals marginal cost. With no externalities, the market equilibrium lands where marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost. Social surplus is then as large as possible and there is no deadweight loss. A monopoly can set its price above marginal cost, making the allocation inefficient. When imperfect knowledge, market power or externalities stop a market allocating resources efficiently, there is market failure. Allocative efficiency is the stricter test: an outcome can be Pareto efficient without it.

nature-econ-191.title: The fundamental theorems of welfare economics
nature-econ-191.text: Two results link markets to efficiency. The first theorem says competitive markets reach a Pareto efficient outcome. It needs complete markets, complete information and perfect competition, in which firms and consumers take prices as given. It is often seen as a formal confirmation of Adam Smith's invisible hand, and Kaushik Basu called it the Invisible Hand Theorem. The outcome need not be fair: many efficient allocations exist, including one where one person owns everything. The second theorem says any Pareto efficient outcome can be reached by a competitive market from suitable starting endowments. It needs stronger conditions, such as convex preferences and convex production sets. Samuelson, building on Bergson, concluded that any desired ethical goal could be reached through one-off taxes or bounties. Oskar Lange's 1942 paper set up the now-traditional pair, one theorem about markets and one about fair shares. Neither theorem guarantees that an equilibrium exists or is unique. Externalities, above all pollution and climate, often break their assumptions. Sometimes a tax on the harm itself, explored in {{ref:nature-pol-088}}, can restore efficiency.

nature-econ-185.title: Distribution: how output and income are shared out
nature-econ-185.text: An economy's output has to end up in someone's hands. Distribution is the way total output, income or wealth is shared out among people, or among the factors of production such as labor, land and capital. Studies of household income often look at the share going to the top or bottom fifth of households, and at what drives those shares. Distribution has been central to political economy since the 19th century, in the work of Adam Smith, David Ricardo and John Stuart Mill. Welfare economics separates how much output is possible from how the resulting income is shared. In neoclassical theory, supply and demand in the markets for labor, land and capital set equilibrium output, income and its distribution. Vilfredo Pareto proposed that income follows a power law, now called the Pareto distribution. The field of {{ref:nature-eecon-059}} treats fair distribution as a goal alongside efficient allocation and a sustainable scale of the economy.

nature-econ-188.title: Equity: fairness in economics
nature-econ-188.text: Fair is not always the same as equal. In economics, equity means fairness: the idea of justice in how wealth, resources and taxes are shared within a society. Economic processes and outcomes should not unduly favor or disadvantage any group or person. Equity is judged separately from efficiency when assessing social welfare, and it is often measured with tools such as the Gini index. It is hard to define, because it depends on social values and would require comparing different people's utility. Peter Corning names three kinds of fairness, equality, equity and reciprocity, that must be balanced for a truly fair society. Economists who run experiments study equity as a dislike of unfair outcomes, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-193}}. Climate policy has tested the idea. Under an early climate treaty, {{ref:nature-clim-056}}, economists argued that equity could be separated from efficiency. It could be handled, for example, through how emission rights are allocated between countries.

nature-econ-200.title: Productive efficiency: no waste on the production line
nature-econ-200.text: An economy can make things cheaply and still make the wrong things. Productive efficiency is a situation in which an economy, using today's technology, cannot make more of one good without making less of another. Every point on the production possibility frontier meets the test. An economy falls inside its frontier when capital or labor sit idle or are put into the wrong industries. In long-run perfect competition, each good is made at the lowest point of its average total cost curve, where marginal cost equals average total cost. Productive efficiency says nothing about making the right mix of goods; misapplied, it can produce the wrong basket faster and cheaper. Monopolies may fall short through what economists call X-inefficiency, though economies of scale can sometimes let them charge less than competitive firms. Better technology and management can push the frontier outward. Data envelopment analysis and stochastic frontier analysis are the most popular ways to estimate it.

nature-econ-172.title: Kaldor–Hicks efficiency: could the winners pay off the losers
nature-econ-172.text: Almost any real policy change leaves somebody worse off, so the Pareto test rarely approves anything. Kaldor–Hicks efficiency is a looser test. A change counts as an improvement if the people who gain could, in principle, fully compensate those who lose, even if they never actually do. Every Pareto improvement passes, but most Kaldor–Hicks improvements are not Pareto improvements. Take a deal that causes pollution. It passes if buyers and sellers would still go ahead while fully compensating the pollution's victims. The Kaldor test asks whether gainers would pay enough to win losers' consent. The Hicks test asks whether losers could not afford to bribe gainers to drop the change. Named after the twentieth-century economists Nicholas Kaldor and John Hicks, the test underpins {{ref:nature-val-001}}. Approving a project whose benefits exceed its costs is the same as requiring that winners could compensate losers. It is also the standard criterion when the costs and benefits of climate change are weighed. Critics dispute why compensation that is never paid should carry moral weight, and note that the test ignores how income is shared.

nature-econ-179.title: Arrow's impossibility theorem: no perfect way to vote
nature-econ-179.text: Three voters face three options, and each voter is perfectly consistent. Yet the majority can prefer A to B, B to C and C to A. Kenneth Arrow generalized this voting paradox of Condorcet's into a startling proof in 1950. No way of combining people's rankings of options into a group ranking can meet all the basic requirements of rational choice. In particular, no such rule can satisfy the principle explored in {{ref:nature-econ-180}}, so no ranked voting system can fully avoid the spoiler effect. The proof founded modern social choice theory. By the 1950s some economists claimed it doomed any attempt to build normative standards in economics. Arrow was milder. Most voting systems do not work badly all the time, he remarked; he only proved that all can work badly at times. There are escape routes. Black showed that if voters and candidates lie along a single left-right spectrum, majority rule can meet all of Arrow's conditions. Rated systems that ask for scores, such as 0–10, escape the theorem by not asking for rankings.

nature-econ-182.title: The capability approach: what people can actually do and be
nature-econ-182.text: Two people with the same income can lead very different lives. The capability approach judges human welfare by what people are actually able to do and be in leading lives they value, not just by their rights or income. Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum developed it in the 1980s as an alternative to traditional welfare economics. Its building blocks are 'functionings': the beings and doings, such as being healthy or safe, that make up a life. Capabilities, in turn, are the combinations of functionings a person can really achieve. Sen argues that utility-based welfare economics ignores how welfare is distributed, neglects rights and freedoms, and is misled by people adapting to bad conditions. Income measures struggle too, because people differ in their ability to turn resources into valuable activities. Nussbaum lists 10 central capabilities, and holds that a decent political order must secure at least a threshold level of each for everyone. The approach led to a UN measure first published in 1990, {{ref:nature-acct-003}}, which weighted health, education and income equally.

nature-econ-208.title: The second best: when fixing one flaw makes things worse
nature-econ-208.text: Free trade is good, says the textbook. Yet liberalizing trade while ignoring an environmental externality can leave welfare lower than doing nothing. Richard Lipsey and Kelvin Lancaster showed why in 1956. Their theory of the second best starts when one condition for an ideal economy cannot be met. The best remaining option may then require moving other conditions away from their ideal values too. If one market distortion cannot be removed, adding another in a linked market may partly offset it and raise efficiency. Fixing a market failure in one sector while an uncorrectable failure remains in a related sector can lower overall efficiency. A common error, the 'fallacy of exhaustive effort', assumes that meeting as many remaining ideal conditions as possible gives the second-best result. Environmental policy uses the insight directly. When an externality itself cannot be taxed, taxing a related product can be the second-best correction.

nature-econ-165.title: The equity–efficiency trade-off: fairness has a price
nature-econ-165.text: Making an economy fairer usually costs something. The equity–efficiency trade-off is the conflict that arises because policies making the economy fairer usually cost some efficiency, so society must choose between the two. The root is simple: redistributing income is costly. Much economic research therefore measures the efficiency losses of tax and transfer programs, which redistribute by their nature. The trade-off sits at the heart of many debates about tax policy, and James Mirrlees began its formal study in 1971. It reaches climate policy too. Because real markets are imperfect, {{ref:nature-pol-253}} may also involve a trade-off between equity and efficiency.

nature-econ-190.title: The excess burden of taxation: the hidden cost of taxes
nature-econ-190.text: A tax costs society more than the money it raises. The extra is the excess burden of taxation, or deadweight loss of taxation. It is the loss a society suffers, beyond the money collected, because taxes or subsidies change how people behave. A sales tax discourages buying the taxed goods. An income tax discourages earning taxed income, and some people leave work or move into the black economy. Subsidies, acting as negative taxes, cause the same waste. Adam Smith first discussed such burdens. Estimates range from 2.5 cents to 30 cents per dollar of revenue on average, and much higher at the margin. As a rule of thumb, the excess burden rises with the square of the tax rate. It can be measured per average dollar raised or for the last dollar raised, the marginal cost of funds. Some taxes distort on purpose. Taxes on alcohol, tobacco and pollution ideally raise the price to include external costs, and such corrective taxes have a negative marginal cost of funds.

nature-econ-161.title: Cardinal social welfare functions: adding up well-being
nature-econ-161.text: Should society take money from the poor and give it to the rich? One kind of social welfare function says yes, if the rich gain more utility than the poor lose. Cardinal social welfare functions take numerical measures of each person's well-being, often income, and turn them into one number for the whole society. The utilitarian or Benthamite version adds up individual utilities. It maximizes total income without caring how that income is shared, which is why it can approve such a transfer. The max-min or Rawlsian version, based on John Rawls, judges society by the welfare of its worst-off member alone. It can be read as society showing an extreme aversion to uncertainty, caring only about the worst position anyone could face. In 1973 Amartya Sen proposed another: average income multiplied by one minus the Gini index.

nature-econ-170.title: Constrained Pareto efficiency: a planner with the same blind spots
nature-econ-170.text: A government cannot fix what it cannot see. Constrained Pareto efficiency is a weaker form of Pareto efficiency. It recognizes that a planner may be unable to improve on an inefficient market outcome, because it faces the same limits as everyone else. It matters when people hold private information, such as a worker's own productivity or a used car's quality. A planner usually has no more information than market participants. So it can only use anonymous rules or rules based on behavior it can observe. If no allowed rule improves on the market outcome, that outcome is called constrained Pareto optimal.

nature-econ-171.title: Pareto efficiency and welfare maximization: two views of one set
nature-econ-171.text: Give every person's utility a positive weight, add the weighted utilities up, and make the total as large as possible. The result is always Pareto efficient, because any Pareto improvement would raise the sum. The link can also run the other way. Takashi Negishi proved that, under certain assumptions, every Pareto efficient allocation maximizes such a weighted sum for some set of positive weights. Choosing the weights then amounts to choosing which efficient outcome to aim for.

nature-econ-169.title: Weak Pareto efficiency: when no one-for-all gain remains
nature-econ-169.text: An outcome is weakly Pareto efficient if no change could make every single person strictly better off. That is a lower bar than the ordinary test. A strong Pareto improvement makes all people strictly better off, while an ordinary Pareto improvement needs only one person strictly better off and the rest no worse. Every strong improvement is also an ordinary one, but not the reverse. So a weakly efficient outcome may still leave room for an ordinary improvement, and may not be fully Pareto efficient.

nature-econ-187.title: The Edgeworth box: a market drawn as a rectangle
nature-econ-187.text: Two people, two goods, one rectangle. The Edgeworth box is a diagram of a tiny market in which each point is one way of splitting the goods between two consumers. Its sides equal the total amounts of the goods, and each consumer's holdings are measured from opposite corners. Francis Ysidro Edgeworth presented it in 1881; Pareto made it the familiar box in 1906. Points where the consumers' indifference curves touch are Pareto optima. Market equilibria sit where both curves touch a common price line, so equilibria are exactly the Pareto optima: the first welfare theorem in pictures.

nature-econ-164.title: Causes of economic inefficiency: why economies fall short
nature-econ-164.text: Economies fall short of Pareto efficiency for many reasons. Imperfect market structures, such as monopoly, monopsony, oligopoly and monopolistic competition, cause inefficiency. So do hidden information, including problems that arise when one party acts for another, and the falling long-run costs of a natural monopoly. Governments add their own: limits on prices and quantities, and regulation arising from government failure. One inefficiency can offset another. If pollution leads to too many tires being made, a tax on tires might restore the efficient amount.

nature-econ-163.title: The four marginal conditions for Pareto efficiency
nature-econ-163.text: Pareto efficiency requires four marginal conditions to hold at once. Every consumer must have the same marginal rate of substitution between any two goods, so no swap between consumers can make both happier. Every producer must have the same marginal rate of transformation between two goods, so shifting production between producers cannot raise total output. A factor such as labor must have the same marginal product at every producer of a good, so moving production cannot cut its cost. Finally, consumers' marginal rates of substitution must equal producers' marginal rates of transformation, so changing the product mix cannot make consumers happier.

nature-econ-166.title: Old welfare economics: when utility could be added up
nature-econ-166.text: The first welfare economists believed utility could be measured and summed. This early neoclassical approach, built by Edgeworth, Sidgwick, Marshall and Pigou, treated utility as measurable and added it up across people. It assumed utility can be measured on a scale, that preferences are fixed and stable, and that each extra unit consumed adds less and less utility. On those assumptions a social welfare function is simply the sum of everyone's utility functions, in Bentham's tradition. It was often inferred that moving income from a rich person to a poor person tends to raise total utility.

nature-econ-167.title: New welfare economics: efficiency without measuring happiness
nature-econ-167.text: Later economists gave up measuring utility. New welfare economics, based on the work of Pareto, Kaldor, Hicks and Scitovsky, judges efficiency without measuring or comparing people's utility. It uses ordinal utility, which only ranks bundles of goods, as on an indifference-curve map. Efficiency and distribution are treated separately: efficiency by the Pareto and Kaldor–Hicks tests, distribution by the choice of social welfare function. The consensus behind it largely collapsed after Arrow's impossibility theorem and related results showed such approaches to be self-contradictory. Murray Rothbard proposed rebuilding welfare economics on 'demonstrated preference', under which only voluntary market exchanges clearly raise welfare.

nature-econ-183.title: The compensation principle: gains that could cover the losses
nature-econ-183.text: The compensation principle favors a change if those who gain could compensate those who lose and still leave nobody worse off. The Pareto criterion is a strict form, in which compensation must actually happen, not just be possible. Many neoclassical economists accept an intervention whenever total gains exceed total losses, paid or not. That is the controversy: when compensation is possible but not paid, some people are simply left as losers. In weighing climate policy, a project that benefits some, compensates the losers and still has something left over is an unambiguous welfare gain.

nature-pol-119.title: Lump-sum taxes: the efficient tax almost nobody uses
nature-pol-119.text: A lump-sum tax is a fixed amount that does not depend on the taxpayer's circumstances, so nothing they do can change what they owe. Because people cannot change their behavior to reduce it, it creates no deadweight loss. The second welfare theorem relies on such lump-sum transfers. The catch is fairness. The tax is regressive: the lower someone's income, the larger the share it takes. A per-person version is called a poll tax. It is rare, because charging poor people such large sums would be politically unacceptable. Switzerland still uses it for some rich foreign residents.

nature-econ-177.title: Missing markets: trades that would help but never happen
nature-econ-177.text: A factory dumps waste into a river and people downstream are harmed. The factory has no reason to count that harm, so no market for pollution forms. That is a missing market: a situation where a competitive market for some good would make everyone better off, yet none exists. Markets go missing for other reasons too, including free riding, difficulty monitoring who causes harm, high costs of making deals, and lack of trust and information. Alternative fuels show the chicken-and-egg version. Stations won't sell a fuel until cars that use it exist, and people won't buy the cars until stations exist. Governments can create the missing conditions. For pollution, a popular fix is assigning clear ownership so the parties can bargain, as in {{ref:nature-econ-629}}. More broadly, economists may try to create missing markets so that efficient trading can happen where none existed before.

openers.efficiency-and-welfare: Is an economy doing well? Economists answer with two questions that sound alike but are not: is it efficient, and is it fair? An economy is efficient when it gets the most of what people want out of the resources it has, and Pareto efficient when no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off. Welfare economics uses those ideas to judge how well off a society is as a whole, resting on two results that link competitive markets to efficiency. Fairness is harder, because deciding how output, income and wealth should be shared draws on ethics, from utilitarianism to theories of justice, and this chapter follows both threads.
